sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Continually improving agents require dynamic interaction feedback beyond static supervision, yet direct real-environment interaction is costly, slow, unsafe, and hard to parallelize. World modeling offers a natural intermediate proxy that allows agents to query lower-cost, more controllable feedback before committing to real actions. Classical world models instantiate this proxy primarily through future physical-state prediction, a formulation useful yet narrow for agents that require actionable feedback beyond raw state transitions. In this work, we conceptualize Agent-Centric Interactive World Proxies, shifting the fundamental paradigm from physical state transitions to agent-usable information transitions, such as execution outcomes, retrieved experiences or skills, and verification signals, broadening the scope of world modeling to provide versatile feedback for continually improving agents. To systematically map this design space, we organize world proxies into six functional forms based on their feedback modalities: dynamics, spatial, execution, memory/experience, skill, and reward/verification proxies, which together characterize the primary ways world modeling serves agent improvement. We further analyze how these proxies empower agents across three progressive levels: L.1 Inference-Time Guidance, where proxy outputs enrich in-context information for superior decisions; L.2 Training-Time Optimization, where proxy outputs yield rewards, critiques, or synthetic rollouts for policy learning; and L.3 Agent-Proxy Co-Evolution, where real-environment evidence continuously updates both the proxy and the agent for co-evolution. Ultimately, this work recasts world modeling into an agent-centric paradigm, establishing a roadmap for building world proxies that empower agents to plan better, learn faster, and evolve continually.

sections.title: 3 Empowerment: How World Proxies Improve Agents . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .
1.1 From Static Supervision to Continual Improvement
sections.content: A truly capable agent does more than finish the task in front of it. It explores the unfamiliar, draws feedback from the world, and turns every success and failure into momentum for the next attempt [157, 203]. Capability of this kind is not granted once at training time; it is earned, again and again, through interaction. Yet most agents today are still taught the way students cram for an exam: from static, offline data such as expert trajectories, human annotations, or supervised fine-tuning corpora [10, 122]. Such data captures patterns that already exist, but it cannot answer back when the agent strikes out on its own. The agents competence is therefore bounded by the distribution it was trained on, and the new information that only active trial and error can reveal stays out of reach [155]. This is the ceiling that genuine self-improvement must break through. How can an agent move beyond static supervision, gather useful feedback through active interaction, and use it to improve without end? The most direct answer is to set the agent loose in the real environment and let it learn from whatever comes back: Agent Action Real Environment Feedback Agent Improvement Figure 2. Basic Agent-Environment Interaction Loop. The agent executes real actions and receives feedback for planning, learning, and improvement. The environment answers with observations, execution results, rewards, or errors, and the agent folds those signals back into its planning, decision making, policy learning, and continual improvement [59, 136, 146]. It is clean loop, and for long time it was the whole story.

sections.title: 1.2 Bottlenecks of Direct Real-Environment Interaction
sections.content: The real environment offers the most faithful feedback, and yet it makes poor sole training ground once an agent needs to err thousands of times, branch across many possibilities at once, and reason several steps ahead before committing. The cracks show up along four recurring axes, collected in Table 1: it is costly, risky, stubbornly backward-looking, and hard to parallelize. 3 Table 1. Bottlenecks of direct real-environment interaction. Bottleneck Explanation Examples Low Training Efficiency and High Cost The agent needs large amount of trial and error, while real interactions are usually expensive and slow. Non-Rollbackable and Risky Interaction Incorrect operations in the real environment are often difficult to undo and may even cause irreversible consequences [94, 198]. Limited Forward-Looking Feedback Difficult to Parallelize Real-environment feedback is usually passive and after-the-fact: it reveals only the outcome of an executed action, making future prediction or multi-step reasoning difficult [125]. Real-environment instances are limited and difficult to replicate at scale like simulated environments [90, 111, 121, 134, 149, 150]. Embodied Agents: robotic trial and error incurs device wear and safety costs [173]. Digital Agents: web, GUI, or game agents consume computation and interaction resources during large-scale sampling [77, 103, 177, 213]. Embodied Agents: robots may collide with or damage objects, and autonomous vehicles may hit pedestrians. Digital Agents: web agents may incorrectly submit, delete, or send information. Embodied Agents: robots cannot easily know in advance whether an action will cause collision. Digital Agents: web or code agents often need to execute before knowing the result. Embodied Agents: physical robot platforms are limited in number. Digital Agents: online services and user environments are difficult to replicate in batches. In short, the real world is indispensable for grounding but ill-suited to scale. To improve efficiently, an agent needs something in between: place to try, to predict, and to reason about what-ifs without paying the full price of real execution.

sections.title: 1.3 World Modeling as an Intermediate Proxy
sections.content: That something is proxy that sits between the agent and the world [57, 146]: Agent World Modeling Real Environment. Figure 3. Agent-Centric World Modeling as an Intermediate Proxy. World Modeling provides lowercost feedback between the Agent and the Real Environment. Crucially, World Modeling here is not stand-in for reality, nor contest to render the most photorealistic future. Its job is humbler and more useful: to act as an intermediate proxy, grounded in the real environment, that hands the agent interaction feedback in cheaper, more controllable, and more predictable form. 4 Concretely, such proxy lets the agent probe its options before committing to any of them. What might happen if take this action? What would see from another viewpoint? What would this command or tool call return? Have faced something like this before, and is the plan safe to run? Each is question the proxy can answer cheaply, and each spares the agent costly or irreversible move in the real world. Seen this way, World Modeling for continually improving agents is no longer confined to next-state prediction; it becomes broader, agent-facing proxy, grounded in real-environment evidence, that can simulate, retrieve, guide, and verify. What makes useful proxy? What separates such proxy from mere simulator or database is what it is optimized for. To genuinely serve continually improving agent, Agent-Centric World Modeling should meet at least three requirements:

sections.title: Key Requirements
sections.content: 1. Agent-Facing Closed Loop: Support agent-initiated queries, actions, or interventions and return conditioned feedback for decision making and improvement. 2. Real-Environment Grounding: Learn from real-environment data, rules, trajectories, or interaction evidence, approximating the outcomes and feedback relevant to agent decisions. 3. Actionable Information Gain: Optimize for better context, safer decisions, more effective exploration, or higher-quality training signals, not only visual realism or prediction accuracy.

sections.title: 2.1 Rethinking World Models
sections.content: To ask where world modeling should go, it helps to recall where it began. classical World Model is usually defined as state transition model [57, 59, 88]: 𝑠𝑡+1 = 𝒲ℳ(𝑠𝑡, 𝑎𝑡). That is, at physical time step 𝑡, the system is in state 𝑠𝑡, executes action 𝑎𝑡, and the World Model predicts the next physical state 𝑠𝑡+1. This form is suitable for robotics, model-based RL, video prediction, and related settings [18, 119, 173]. Its core focus is: Current State + Action Future State. In other words, traditional World Model traces single thread of state transitions along physical time. Even modern self-supervised variants that predict in learned latent space [194] rather than in raw pixels [5, 6] inherit this backbone: state goes in, an action is applied, and future comes out. For continually improving agent, however, the feedback worth having reaches well past the next state. Over the course of solving task, such an agent may need to: simulate the result of an action, command, API call, or tool call [52, 106, 148]; retrieve relevant information from memory, experience, or failure cases [123, 124, 140]; query reusable skills or sub-policies for the current task [2, 98, 157]; verify whether plan, trajectory, or action is safe and feasible [32, 99, 112]; obtain reward, critique, preference, or error-diagnosis signals for training [30, 122, 128]. What unites these is the kind of answer they return. None is simply next state; each is different species of information, consequence, memory, skill, judgment, that the agent can immediately act on. Thus the classical World Model is an indispensable starting point, but only starting point: it captures one mechanism of Agent-World interaction, not the full repertoire continually improving agent relies on.

sections.title: 2.2 From World Model to World Proxy
sections.content: To embrace this wider set of interactions, we generalize the World Model into World Proxy. The move is less replacement than broadening of the same core idea: an intermediate mechanism, grounded in the real environment, that supplies feedback the agent would otherwise have to win through direct execution. What changes is the reach. World Proxy need not stop at predicting the next state; it may also simulate execution results, retrieve experience, offer skill guidance, or verify and evaluate behavior [52, 99, 124, 157]. Figure 4. From World Model to World Proxy. World Proxy is an agent-facing proxy layer that may instantiate as dynamics prediction, spatial synthesis, execution simulation, memory retrieval, skill guidance, or reward / verification feedback. Concretely, this broader view stretches the classical definition along three axes, summarized in Table 2: 6 Table 2. From environment-centric prediction to agent-centric interaction modeling. Rethinking From To Key Idea Physical Time Step Interaction Step 𝑡 𝑡 + 1 ℓ ℓ + State Transition Information Transition External Condition Agent-Initiated Interaction 𝑠𝑡 𝑠𝑡+1 𝑠ℓ 𝑠ℓ+1 external 𝑢ℱ ℓ Agent interaction does not always advance physical time. It may query viewpoint, simulate execution, retrieve experience, or verify plan. We use interaction step ℓ to describe each Agent-World interaction. The output of World Proxy is not limited to next-state prediction. It can be viewed as an information transition, such as new observation, execution result, retrieved memory or skill, reward, verification feedback, or other agent-usable information. The interaction condition should be agent-initiated: query, action, or intervention actively proposed by the Agent according to its goal and context, rather than only an externally given condition. Note. ℱ denotes different proxy functions, such as dynamics prediction, spatial rendering, execution simulation, memory retrieval, skill guidance, and reward / verification. Therefore, the key question for an Agent-Centric World Proxy is not only whether the prediction is accurate, but: What new information will the agent obtain after this interaction? In this sense, the output of World Proxy should be organized as agent-usable feedback, rather than only as an environmental state. The shift is subtle but freeing: memory lookup, code execution, and reward estimate can all be treated as one move of the same game, each delivering information the agent did not possess an instant earlier [30, 140, 148].

sections.content: Pulling these threads together, we can now state the idea precisely. We define an Agent-Centric World Proxy as: An Agent-Centric World Proxy is an environment-grounded proxy that models or predicts information transitions conditioned on agent-initiated interactions, aiming to provide information gain for agent improvement. Formally, it is expressed as: where: 𝑠ℓ+1 = 𝒲𝒫 (𝑠ℓ, 𝑢ℱ ℓ ) , 𝑠ℓ 𝒮. ℓ: interaction step, representing the ℓ-th interaction between the Agent and the World Proxy, not limited to physical time; 𝒮: information state space, generalized space that may include physical state, observation, memory, knowledge, execution result, verification, guidance, and more; ℱ: proxy function, such as dynamics prediction, spatial rendering, execution simulation, memory retrieval, skill guidance, or reward / verification; 7 𝑢ℱ ℓ : the query, action, or intervention actively proposed by the Agent under specific proxy function; 𝑠ℓ+1: the feedback returned by the World Proxy, such as future state, novel observation, execution result, retrieved memory / skill, reward, or verification result. single prediction, though, is not yet improvement. To serve continually improving agent, the proxy cannot remain one-shot oracle; it must close the loop with the agent [41, 140, 157]: Agent 𝑢ℱ ℓ 𝒲𝒫 𝑠ℓ+1 Agent. Figure 5. Agent-in-the-Loop World Proxy. The agent queries the World Proxy, which predicts, simulates, retrieves, or verifies the resulting information transition and returns feedback for agent improvement. At the ℓ-th interaction step, this loop can be divided into four steps: Step 1: Agent proposes an interaction The Agent actively proposes an interaction request 𝑢ℱ state, and other conditions. ℓ according to its current goal, context Step 2: World Proxy predicts information transition The World Proxy predicts or generates feedback conditioned on the current information state 𝑠ℓ and the agent interaction 𝑢ℱ ℓ . Step 4: Agent uses feedback for improvement The Agent uses the feedback for planning, decision making, policy learning, or continual improvement. Run once, this is single prediction; iterated over many steps, it becomes trajectory of improvement, since each answer quietly reshapes the next question the Agent thinks to ask.

sections.title: 2.4 What Makes a Good World Proxy?
sections.content: Not every intermediate module is an effective World Proxy. For continually improving agents, good World Proxy should provide feedback that is grounded, controllable, actionable, scalable, and forward-looking within the agents closed loop. Table 3. Criteria for effective World Proxies. Criterion Meaning Groundedness Controllability Relies on real environment data, rules, trajectories, or interaction evidence, not detached generation. Supports agent-initiated queries, actions, or interventions and returns corresponding feedback. Feedback Usefulness Improves planning, decision making, policy learning, or continual improvement. Cost and Scalability Reduces real-world interaction cost while scaling safely across tasks and settings. Forward-Looking Ability Anticipates outcomes, counterfactuals, or risks before real execution. In practice, useful World Proxies must balance real-environment grounding, scalability, and actionable feedback; proxies that drift too far from grounding soon stop being useful, and confidently wrong ones can be worse than none [153].

sections.title: Takeaway
sections.content: 1. From World Model to World Proxy: Extending beyond future-state prediction to spatial rendering, execution simulation, memory retrieval, skill guidance, reward modeling, and verification. 2. From Realism to Information Gain: Moving beyond prediction accuracy to prioritize agent-usable feedback for planning, decision making, learning, and continual improvement. 3. From one-shot prediction to closed loop: Use agent-initiated interaction and proxy feedback to drive iterative improvement.

sections.title: 3 Empowerment: How World Proxies Improve Agents
sections.content: With the World Proxy defined, the obvious question is what it actually buys us: How can World Proxies help an Agent plan, learn, and evolve? One way to answer is to grade the world model by its own intrinsic capability, as Chu et al. [31] do: L.1 Predictor: one-step / local transition prediction; L.2 Simulator: long-horizon, action-conditioned rollout; L.3 Evolver: world model self-reflection. 9 Figure 6. L1 to L3 World Proxies for Agent Improvement. L1 augments inference-time context, L2 provides training signals, and L3 enables Agent-Proxy co-evolution. These levels grade the world models own competence. Our question is orthogonal: not how capable the model is in isolation, but how much better it makes the agent. We deliberately reuse the L1-L3 shorthand for this agent-centric axis, so the two scales rhyme without being identical; Table 4 sets them side by side to keep the two readings distinct. World-Proxy-Driven Agent Improvement We take an agent-centric perspective: instead of asking how powerful the World Model itself is, we ask how World Proxy drives Agent improvement. This leads to three levels: L.1 Inference-Time Guidance Proxy Role: augments inference-time context. Agent Effect: better decisions. L.2 Training-Time Optimization Proxy Role: provides reward, verification, or simulation signals. Agent Effect: optimizes the policy. L.3 Agent-Proxy Co-Evolution Proxy Role: closes the Agent-Proxy-Environment loop. Agent Effect: continual co-evolution. 10 Table 4. Two orthogonal readings of the L1-L3 shorthand: world models intrinsic capability [31] versus the agent-centric empowerment used in this article. The rungs align in spirit, not in definition. Level Intrinsic WM Capability (Chu et al.) Agent-Centric Empowerment (Ours) L.1 L.2 L.3 Predictor: one-step / local transition prediction Inference-Time Guidance: enrich context for better decisions Simulator: long-horizon, action-conditioned rollout Training-Time Optimization: reshape the agent policy Evolver: world-model self-reflection Agent-Proxy Co-Evolution: continual mutual improvement Read together, the three levels form ladder of increasing commitment. L1 leaves the agent untouched and merely informs its next move; L2 reaches into the agents parameters and rewrites its policy; L3 lets agent and proxy reshape each other over time. Capability grows at every rung, and so does the burden of proof on the proxy, because the deeper its feedback reaches, the more mistake costs.

sections.title: 3.1 L1: Inference-Time Guidance
sections.content: Figure 7. L1 Inference-Time Guidance via World Proxy. The Agent queries the World Proxy, which retrieves, simulates, or verifies relevant information. The returned guidance is added to the Agents context for better inference-time decisions. We begin with the lightest touch. At L1, the World Proxy never alters the Agents parameters; it simply hands over extra context, experience, skill, or verification feedback at inference time, so the decision the Agent is about to make is better-informed one [52, 62, 85, 169, 188, 189]. Because nothing is retrained, L1 is cheap and fully reversible; its ceiling, though, is the agents existing competence, since it can only recombine what the agent already knows. Formally: 11 ℓ+1 = 𝒲𝒫 (𝑠𝑎𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑡 𝑠𝑔𝑢𝑖𝑑𝑒 ℓ , 𝑢ℱ ℓ ) , 𝑠𝑎𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑡+ ℓ = 𝑠𝑎𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑡 ℓ 𝑠𝑔𝑢𝑖𝑑𝑒 ℓ+1 . 𝑠𝑔𝑢𝑖𝑑𝑒 ℓ+1 denotes guidance returned by the World Proxy, and denotes adding it to the Here, Agents current context for information augmentation.

sections.title: Process
sections.content: The flow runs in one direction, from the agents question to richer context for its very next move; Fig. 7 gives the corresponding visual layout: Agent Query Proxy Retrieval / Simulation / Verification Guidance Augmented Context Agent Decision

sections.title: Implementations
sections.content: Memory / Skill Retrieval: retrieves historical experience, strategies, skills, or tool-use rules according to the current task [124, 135, 140, 144, 157, 193]; Execution Simulation: simulates the result of an action or action sequence before real execution [52, 132, 148]; Verification Feedback: determines whether the current plan / action is safe, feasible, and consistent with constraints [32, 99, 112]. In practice, this is the agent looking before it leaps: web agent about to click Purchase can first ask the proxy to imagine the resulting page, then revise its plan if that page shows an error or an unintended charge, all without touching the live site [52]. Key Point L1 lets the Agent gain richer context within the current episode, so it can see more, reason more accurately, and act more robustly.

sections.title: 3.2 L2: Training-Time Optimization
sections.content: L2 raises the stakes. The World Proxy now does more than whisper context at inference time; it serves as reward model, verifier, critic, or simulator, producing the training signals that reshape the Agents policy itself [28, 30, 32, 99, 122]. This lifts the agents ceiling rather than merely its current context, but the gain is only as trustworthy as the signal behind it: biased reward quietly teaches biased behavior. Formally: 𝑠𝑜𝑝𝑡 ℓ+1 = 𝒲𝒫 (𝑠𝑎𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑡 ℓ , 𝑢ℱ ℓ ) , agent+ = 𝑇𝑟𝑎𝑖𝑛 (agent, 𝑠𝑜𝑝𝑡 ℓ+1) . 𝑠𝑜𝑝𝑡 ℓ+1 denotes training signals generated by the World Proxy, such as reward, verification, Here, critique, or simulated rollouts. These signals can be converted into objectives such as SFT, DPO [128], PPO [137], or GRPO [138]. Compared with L1, the key change in L2 is: Proxy Output as Context Proxy Output as Training Signal 12 Figure 8. L2 Training-Time Optimization Driven by World Proxy. The Agent generates rollouts, which are evaluated, verified, or simulated by the World Proxy. The resulting reward, critique, preference, or verification signal is converted into training objective to optimize the Agent policy.

sections.title: Process
sections.content: Now the loop bends back into learning: the proxys verdict on rollout becomes gradient on the policy rather than hint for the moment; Fig. 8 gives the corresponding visual layout. Agent Rollout Proxy Verification / Simulation Reward / Critique / Preference Training Objective Agent Policy Optimization

sections.title: Implementations
sections.content: Proxy-as-Reward: The World Proxy or verifier scores trajectories to form rewards [10, 30, 122]. Proxy-as-Critic: Identifies failure causes and outputs critiques, error diagnoses, or constraint violations [109, 112, 200]. Proxy-as-Simulator: Generates synthetic trajectories or constructs preference pairs for DPO / RLHF / GRPO [28, 161, 168]. Proxy-Guided Curriculum: Generates harder or more targeted tasks based on the Agents current failure modes [167, 206]. In practice, the agents own rollouts become training fuel: the proxy scores, verifies, or replays them into synthetic trajectories and preference pairs, so policy can be optimized at scale that collecting real interactions could never reach [28, 168]. 13 Key Point L2 upgrades the World Proxy from an inference-time advisor to training-time judge, teacher, or simulated environment, directly optimizing the Agent policy.

sections.title: 3.3 L3: Agent-Proxy Co-Evolution
sections.content: Figure 9. L3 Agent-Proxy Co-Evolution. Real-environment evidence updates the World Proxy, while useful proxy knowledge is distilled back into the Agent policy for continual improvement. L3 completes the arc by closing continual loop among the Agent, the World Proxy, and the real environment. Real trajectories, failures, and fresh discoveries update the proxy; the sharpened proxy then guides, verifies, and trains the Agent, so both improve together rather than one after the other [41, 130, 140, 157]. This is the most powerful rung, but it also requires machinery that keeps proxy and policy aligned as both change. Formally: 𝑠𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑥𝑦 ℓ+1 = 𝒲𝒫 (𝑠𝑎𝑔𝑒𝑛𝑡 ℓ , 𝑢ℱ ℓ ) , (agent+, 𝒲𝒫+) = 𝐶𝑜𝐸𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑣𝑒 (agent, 𝒲𝒫, 𝑠𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑥𝑦 ℓ+1 , 𝑠𝑒𝑛𝑣 ℓ+1) 𝑠𝑝𝑟𝑜𝑥𝑦 ℓ+1 denotes proxy feedback, 𝑠𝑒𝑛𝑣 Here, updates both the Agent and the World Proxy. ℓ+1 denotes real-environment evidence, and 𝐶𝑜𝐸𝑣𝑜𝑙𝑣𝑒()

sections.content: The loop now uses real-environment gaps as the update signal; Fig. 9 gives the corresponding visual layout: Agent Rollout Proxy Prediction / Verification Real-Environment Evidence Disagreement / Error Diagnosis Update Proxy + Distill to Agent Co-Evolution

sections.title: Implementations
sections.content: Proxy Agent Internalization: memory, skills, constraints, verification rules, or reward signals are distilled into Agent parameters or policies, turning external feedback into internal capability [2, 98, 157]. Agent Proxy Update: real interaction trajectories, effective experiences, failure cases, and environmental feedback update the World Proxys memory, skill library, verifier, simulator, or reward model [20, 41, 140]. In practice, picture web agent whose every deployment both draws on the proxys predictions and feeds fresh trajectories back into it: proxy and policy are retrained in tandem, each cycle shrinking the gap between what the agent imagines and what the world actually returns [41]. Key Point L3 makes the World Proxy more than static tool: it becomes co-evolving partner that is continually updated through real-environment evidence. Worked Example: One Web Agent up the Ladder To see the three levels as one continuum rather than three separate tricks, follow single web agent completing multi-step online purchase, and watch the same execution proxy deepen its role at each rung: L.1 Guidance. Before clicking Purchase, the agent asks the proxy to imagine the resulting page; if that page shows an error or an unintended charge, it revises its plan, without ever touching the live site [52]. L.2 Optimization. Those imagined rollouts are not discarded: the proxy scores and replays them into synthetic trajectories and preference pairs, and the agents policy is optimized on this fabricated experience at scale live interaction could never reach [28]. L.3 Co-Evolution. Once deployed, the agents real trajectories flow back to retrain the proxy, and the sharpened proxy in turn yields better guidance and training signal, each cycle shrinking the gap between what the agent imagines and what the web actually returns [41]. One agent, one proxy function, three escalating roles: advisor, teacher, and partner.

sections.title: Takeaway
sections.content: World Proxies empower agents through three progressive levels: L.1 Inference-Time Guidance. The World Proxy provides memory, skill, simulation, or verification feedback to enrich inference-time context and support better decisions. L.2 Training-Time Optimization. The World Proxy acts as reward model, critic, verifier, or simulator, generating training signals that directly optimize the Agent policy. L.3 Agent-Proxy Co-Evolution. Real-environment evidence updates the World Proxy, whose knowledge is distilled back into the Agent for continual improvement.

sections.title: 4 Instantiations: Functional Forms of Agent-Centric World Proxies
sections.content: If Section 3 asked how World Proxy helps, this section asks in what form it appears. The single symbol ℱ in our definition quietly stands in for whole family of proxy functions; here we unpack it into six concrete forms: dynamics prediction, spatial observation, execution simulation, memory retrieval, skill guidance, and reward/verification. Each has grown into research area in its own right, and several recent surveys map them in depth [44, 95, 151, 215]. Figure 10. Functional forms of Agent-Centric World Proxies. World Proxy may simulate dynamics, render spatial observations, predict execution outcomes, retrieve memory, suggest skills, or provide reward / verification feedback.

sections.title: 4.1 Overview
sections.content: The six forms differ less in their machinery than in the question each one answers for the agent. Table 5 lines them up at glance, pairing every function with the input it consumes, the slice of the world it stands in for, and what it hands back; we then take each in turn.

sections.title: Meaning
sections.content: 𝑠ℓ+1, 𝑟ℓ+1 = 𝒲𝒫dyn (𝑠ℓ, 𝑢dyn ℓ ) . The Dynamics Proxy is the classical form of World Model. Given the current state, history, and an agent action or future query, it predicts the future state and may also predict reward. It is the 16 proxy in its most literal sense, learned stand-in for the dynamics of the environment, and the closest of the six forms to the textbook world model. Table 5. sections.title: 4.8 Putting It Together: Functions Meet Levels
sections.content: The two axes of this article are orthogonal: any proxy function (Section 4) can empower an agent at any level (Section 3). Reading the six functions against L1-L3 turns the design space into simple map, with representative systems in each cell  (Table 6)  . The mapping is illustrative rather than exclusive, since many systems span more than one level, and the sparser cells mark territory that remains largely open. Two patterns stand out. Reading down column shows that single level admits many functional realizations; reading across row shows that the same function can graduate from advisor to teacher to partner as it climbs L1 to L3. sections.title: Takeaway
sections.content: Different proxy functions, one purpose: agent-usable feedback. Beyond future-state prediction: World Proxy may predict dynamics, render spatial observations, simulate execution, retrieve experience, suggest skills, or provide reward / verification feedback. Function defines feedback type: dynamics, spatial, execution, memory, skill, and verification proxies differ in what information transition they approximate for the Agent. Actionability is the common criterion: regardless of function, the output should help the Agent plan, decide, learn, verify, or continually improve.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion: Quo Vadis, World Modeling?
sections.content: We opened with question, so let us close with an answer. For most of its history, world modeling has been pursued as the art of predicting the world: given state and an action, render the next frame as faithfully as possible [36]. This article has argued for quieter but consequential shift, from predicting the world to serving the agent. Once the goal becomes continual improvement, the right object is no longer state predictor but an Agent-Centric World Proxy: an environment-grounded mechanism that returns the information transition an agent needs, whether future state, rendered view, execution result, retrieved memory or skill, or verdict on plan. That reframing organized the rest of the story. We saw why real environments alone cannot carry continual improvement, what changes when physical state transitions become interactive information transitions, how proxies empower agents across L.1 inference-time guidance, L.2 training-time optimization, and L.3 Agent-Proxy co-evolution, and in what forms they appear: dynamics, spatial, execution, memory, skill, and reward / verification. The unifying thread is not visual realism for its own sake, but actionable information gain. The same reframing also sharpens the open problems. proxy is only as useful as it is trustworthy, and trust remains the hardest part to guarantee.

sections.title: Open Challenges
sections.content: 1. Fidelity and the limits of imagination. Generative models can look convincing while violating the dynamics they claim to model [56, 78, 80, 153]. Errors compound over long rollouts; calibrated uncertainty, not just sharper pixels, is the missing ingredient. 2. Knowing when to trust the proxy. An agent must decide, online, whether to act on proxy feedback or return to the real environment. Today agents rarely make that judgment well [125]; treating the proxy as an oracle invites silent failure. 3. Reward hacking and safety. When the proxy becomes the reward or verifier (L2), the agent is incentivized to exploit blind spots. The same sandbox that makes risky exploration safe also opens new attack surface [94, 101, 178, 180, 198]. 4. Evaluation that measures information gain. Current benchmarks score realism, fidelity, controllability, or human-aligned quality [87, 91, 127], but still grade the proxy in isolation. We need agent-centric benchmarks: did the feedback help the agent plan, learn, or improve? None of these are reasons for pessimism; they are the agenda. Each becomes tractable once we stop asking world model to be perfect mirror and start asking it to be useful interlocutor, one whose answers are grounded, calibrated, and continually corrected by contact with reality. The L3 loop, where real-environment evidence keeps the proxy honest and the proxy keeps the agent improving, is as much safety mechanism as learning one. So, quo vadis? We expect the most valuable world models of the coming years to be judged less by how vividly they dream and more by how much better they make the agents that query them. If this article nudges the conversation from building world simulators toward building world proxies that agents can learn from, it will have served its purpose.
